## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_editor_state(include_schema: true) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- resolving-merge-conflicts: Use when you need to resolve an in-progress git merge/rebase conflict.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- releases: CipherBox v2 release and staging-deploy mechanics — release-please layout, the two version surfaces, staging tag pipeline, and the v1 freeze. Use when cutting a release, deploying to staging, or touching release/versioning config.
- crypto-privacy-review: Review code for cryptographic security, generate test cases and edge cases
- resolve-pr-reviews: Resolve PR Review Comments
- ship: Ship
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.prompt:
You are shipping ONE pull request in the CipherBox repo. You are in an isolated git worktree forked from local `main` at `bf8bc74cb`. Read `AGENTS.md` and `CONTEXT.md` first — they are binding.

BRANCH: `chore/719-retro-audit-sweep`
PR TITLE: `chore: sweep the retro-audit cleanup backlog` (NO parentheses anywhere in the title — a commitlint rule rejects them).

SCOPE — implement all seven, then `Closes #997`, `Closes #998`, `Closes #999`, `Closes #1000`, `Closes #1001`, `Closes #1002`, `Closes #1003`, `Closes #719` in the PR body. Read each issue with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh issue view <N>` before starting it.

1. **#997** — `fanout_get_verify` at `crates/engine/src/net/fanout.rs:91` returns `(u64, bytes)`, forcing callers to rebuild the `VerifiedRecord` it already had. Return the `VerifiedRecord`. Callers to update: `net/liveness.rs:184` (`eol_republish`), `net/publish.rs:210`, `net/resolve.rs:191`, `net/pointer_fetch.rs:35`, `settings.rs:320`, `sync/drain.rs:1214`; re-export at `net/mod.rs:41`. `VerifiedRecord` is already public from `crates/core/src/ipns/record.rs`.
2. **#998** — route ALL floor reads through the `floor::*` wrappers. `gate/floor.rs:159` has `sequence_floor`; direct seam readers bypassing it are `net/publish.rs:175`, `facade.rs:5145`/`:5178`/`:5310`, `settings.rs:317`. Second half: hoist the engine's constant-time compare onto core — the helper is `ct_eq_32` in `crates/engine/src/secret_util.rs` (the issue calls it `ct_eq_secret`; the name has drifted), new home is `crates/core/src/suite/secret.rs` on `SecretBytes`. ~8 engine call sites: `session.rs`, `grants/owner_entry.rs`, `grants/accept.rs`, `grants/create.rs`, `gate/adoption.rs`, `rotation/cascade.rs`, `rotation/reseal.rs`.
3. **#999** — delete the dead `ApiError::NotAuthenticated` (`api/error.rs:34`,`:73`) and the unused `ChallengeResponse.expires_at` (`api/types.rs:67-70`). CAUTION: `NotAuthenticated` IS referenced by tests at `sync/drain.rs:2234`/`:2262`/`:2287` — re-point those, do not just delete and leave them broken. The `post_json_authed` helper in the issue is optional; use judgement.
4. **#1000** — `commit_floors` returns a `Vec<u64>` no production caller consumes (`seams/floor_store.rs:55` default impl; sole prod caller `gate/floor.rs:247` discards it). BEFORE changing it, check `testkit/conformance/floor_store.rs:80`/`:90`/`:130` — the conformance kit ASSERTS the return value, so dropping it means rewriting those assertions. If the conformance assertions are load-bearing for a real invariant, say so in the PR body and keep the return. Other impls: `crates/desktop-seams/src/floor_store.rs:175`, `testkit/fakes/floor_store.rs:66`, `crates/engine/tests/floor_atomic.rs:134`, doc at `crates/wasm/src/seams_bridge.rs:104`.
5. **#1001** — remove the zeroizing `Drop` on `IpnsRecord` at `crates/core/src/ipns/record.rs:374-386`; it zeroizes data that is published to IPFS, so it protects nothing. Note this file is in `crates/core` despite the issue's `comp:engine` label.
6. **#1002** — hoist the triplicated `hex_lower` Debug formatter from `crates/core/src/suite/{ecdsa.rs:134,ed25519.rs:104,x25519.rs:134}` into one helper in `crates/core/src/suite/mod.rs`.
7. **#1003** — add a `SecretField` newtype (or macro) for the four hand-rolled redacted-`Debug` + non-constant-time-`PartialEq` pairs in `crates/core/src/seal/grant.rs`: `GrantBlobPayload` (:144/:159), `OverrideSeedPayload` (:300/:310), `OwnerWriteBlobPayload` (:433/:443), `HistoryLinkPayload` (:669/:679). Home it in `crates/core/src/suite/secret.rs` alongside #998's ct-eq hoist. This one genuinely depends on #998 landing first — do #998 before #1003 within this branch.

Suggested internal order: 1001, 1002 (trivial) → 999 → 997 → 998 → 1003 → 1000.

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- `cargo fmt --all` — NEVER scope it to `-p`; the CI gate is `cargo fmt --all --check` and scoping it has broken CI twice.
- Do NOT set or share `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` with any other worktree — it silently reuses stale test binaries.
- `cargo check --workspace` does NOT build wasm32. Since you touch `crates/core` and seam-adjacent engine code, also run `cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (confirm the crate name from the workspace manifest) or the equivalent, or you will break the Core KAT and Client Browser Suite legs while the workspace check stays green.
- Rule 8 of AGENTS.md: encode/decode fail-closed symmetry. Any decode-side hard reject needs a matching RELEASE-ACTIVE encode-side `Err` — never `debug_assert!`. This is a recurring P1 in review.
- Zeroize only at the terminal owner; a callee must never zero a caller-owned buffer.
- Comments explain WHY and stay short. No absence-justifying comments (prose about paths NOT in the code) and no apologia defending code this diff does not modify. These get flagged by every reviewer.
- Conventional Commits. Commit signing goes through the 1Password SSH agent, which can hang — run `git commit` unsandboxed with a `timeout` guard, and NEVER pass `--no-gpg-sign`.
- Always prefix gh with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- No Claude/AI attribution and no session link in the PR body.

REVIEW GATES — mandatory, run each on your own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and FOLD REAL FINDINGS BACK IN before you finish:
1. `/simplify`
2. `/security-review`
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — REQUIRED here; this diff touches `crates/core` primitives, constant-time comparison, secret redaction, and zeroization.
If a slash-command skill is unavailable, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead. Never skip a gate.

FINISH BY: opening the PR as a **DRAFT** (`gh pr create --draft`). Do not mark it ready and do not request a CodeRabbit review — review timing is managed centrally to conserve quota.

REPORT BACK: PR number and URL, per-issue status, the #1000 conformance decision and your reasoning, anything you could not complete and why, and the exact test/check commands you ran with their results. Report failures honestly — do not claim green if it is not.

---
name: project-v2-hot-file-contention-caps-parallelism
description: Engine PR parallelism is capped by a handful of hot files, not by issue count — batch by file ownership
metadata:
  type: project
---

When batching v2 issues into parallel PRs, the binding constraint is hot-file contention, not the
number of actionable issues. Measured 2026-08-04 against a cleared board (0 open PRs, 59 actionable
leaves): a handful of files are touched by nearly every engine cluster.

- `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` and `crates/engine/tests/write_plane.rs` — touched by almost every
  engine issue
- `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs` — settings, op-queue, pin-provider, device-state clusters
- `crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs` + `seams/floor_store.rs` — the #719 cleanups AND the
  per-account floor namespacing
- `crates/wasm/src/host.rs` — every seam-shape or config-plumbing change
- `packages/client/src/seams/types.ts` + `http.ts`, `apps/web/src/engine/snapshotStore.ts`,
  `packages/client/src/leaderRelay.ts`

**Why:** facade.rs is 5000+ lines so different functions usually auto-merge, but signature/shape
changes ripple. The recurring failure is the semantic merge conflict in
[[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]] — two PRs both MERGEABLE that break main's compile
pairwise.

**How to apply:** batch so each PR *owns* its hot files exclusively, and sequence any PR carrying a
signature change ahead of everything touching its callers. Group small issues that collide on the
same interface into ONE PR rather than trying to parallelize them — this also conserves the
CodeRabbit quota (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]]). Reserve worktree isolation
for the batches that genuinely run concurrently.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:

## Scope — part 1 of 2

#1015 covers grant invites end to end: ephemeral-key grant blobs, a ledger expiry field, claim-to-grant conversion, and bearer write-link flagging. The issue itself states this splits into two PRs.

**Ship part 1 only: the ephemeral-key grant blob plus the ledger expiry field.** Leave claim conversion and bearer write-link flagging for part 2. Use `Part of #1015` in the body, NOT `Closes`.

## What already exists — do NOT rebuild

`crates/engine/src/grants/` is ~2,600 lines, all landed: `create.rs`, `accept.rs`, `ledger.rs`, `child_index.rs`, `revocation.rs`, `owner_entry.rs`, `contact.rs`. Invites are the only greenfield part — today only doc-comment mentions at `grants/create.rs:23` and `grants/mod.rs:8`.

The HPKE ephemeral plumbing you need already exists in `crates/core/src/seal/grant.rs` — the seal functions already take an `ephemeral_scalar: &[u8; 32]` parameter (see the existing `GrantBlobPayload`, `OverrideSeedPayload`, `OwnerWriteBlobPayload`, `HistoryLinkPayload` seal paths). Follow that established shape rather than inventing a new one.

## Conventions that just changed — follow the NEW ones

1. **Secret-bearing fields use `SecretBytes`.** As of `31f06c7e`, `crates/core/src/suite/secret.rs` provides `SecretBytes` with a redacting `Debug` and a constant-time `PartialEq`, plus a free `ct_eq`. Any new payload type you add must derive over `SecretBytes` — do NOT hand-roll a redacted `Debug` or a `PartialEq`, and do NOT write a new `SecretField`-style newtype. `crates/engine/src/secret_util.rs` was deleted; `ct_eq_32` no longer exists.
2. **Redaction tests are whole-string goldens, not marker counts.** PR #1021 is in flight and converts these: the old style counted `SecretBytes(redacted)` occurrences against a per-type constant, which a field added later as a raw `[u8; 32]` slips past silently. Write your new tests as whole-string goldens so any added field of any type breaks the test and forces a redaction decision. Do not copy the marker-count style you may still see in `main`.
3. `hex_lower` now lives once, at `cipherbox_core::hex::lower`. `crates/engine/src/hex.rs` is gone.

## Security requirements — an invite is a bearer credential

This is the highest-risk surface in the current batch. Treat it accordingly.

- **Entropy is injected.** Ephemeral keypair generation MUST come through a seam, never a direct RNG call in core or engine logic. Match the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention and cover it with a test that fires in a release build.
- Zeroize only at the terminal owner; a callee must never zero a caller-owned buffer.
- Never log key material, seeds, or invite secrets.

Agent on `feat/1014-rotation-resolvers-and-publishers` is editing `crates/engine/src/rotation/` and `crates/engine/src/net/`, and touches ONE line in `crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs` (a stale doc pointer at `:16`). Stay out of that line. Do not coordinate with that branch; just expect a possible small rebase.

- Comments explain WHY and stay short. No absence-justifying comments, no apologia for code this diff does not modify.
- Conventional Commits. Commit signing goes through the 1Password SSH agent, which can hang — run `git commit` unsandboxed with a `timeout` guard, and NEVER pass `--no-gpg-sign`. `--no-verify` is acceptable for Rust-only commits since this worktree has no `node_modules`.
- Always prefix gh with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- No Claude/AI attribution and no session link in the PR body.

## Review gates — mandatory

Run each on your own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and FOLD REAL FINDINGS BACK IN before finishing:
1. `/simplify`
2. `/security-review`
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — this is the one that matters most here. New sealed payload types, bearer credentials, ephemeral key handling, expiry enforcement.
If a slash-command skill is unavailable, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead. Never skip a gate.

# Security review: `feat/1014-rotation-resolvers-and-publishers`

Reviewed the effective diff (`git diff $(git merge-base main HEAD)` — the branch's two commits **plus** the uncommitted working-tree changes, which are a further ~250 lines the three-dot diff alone misses).

Two HIGH findings, both confirmed against the code rather than inferred. One is fixed and covered by a regression test; the other is a design gap too large to fix inside this gate.

---

## Vuln 1 — Rule 8 violation: the publisher signs and publishes a scope root its own adoption gate always rejects — `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:382`

- **Severity: HIGH** · Category: `fail_closed_asymmetry` (AGENTS.md rule 8) · **Confidence 10 — reproduced**
- **Description:** `reseal_scope_root` signed the write-body's *structure signature* at `seeds.write_epoch`. The adoption gate recomputes **every** structure-signature preimage at the envelope's **read** epoch (`crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:455-459` captures `epoch = candidate.envelope.epoch`; write-body at `:488-493`). Every other structure signs at `read_epoch` — including the owner-write-blob, whose identical dual-epoch convention (AAD at the write epoch, signature at the read epoch) is spelled out at `reseal.rs:290-294`. The write-body was the lone deviation.
- **Exploit scenario:** `rotate_scope` bumps `read_epoch` while `write_epoch` stays fixed, so the two diverge on **every** read rotation. Before this PR the publisher was faked, so the bug was inert; this PR wires the real `ScopeRootPublisher`, so the first production revocation rotation signs and publishes a scope root that fails gate stage 3 (`structure-signature-invalid`, whole-record, `#39 D3`) for **every reader including the owner, permanently**. Since a signed record cannot be unpublished and floors are monotonic, the scope root is bricked — revocation cannot complete and the subtree becomes unreachable.
- **Why no test caught it:** `publish_scope_root` gates only the *current* record, never the one it publishes; `a_resealed_root_lands_at_the_new_epoch_carrying_its_new_section` decodes the published block but never re-gates it; and every gated fixture uses `read_epoch == write_epoch == 1`, which masks the divergence.
- **Fix applied:** `reseal.rs:382` now signs at `read_epoch`, with a one-line note tying it to the owner-write-blob's stated rationale. Added `a_published_cut_re_adopts_through_this_builds_own_gate` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:790`), which publishes a cut with `read_epoch != write_epoch` and re-adopts it through the real gate — it fails with `Err(Rejected)` before the fix, passes after. This closes the general rule-8 hole too: the publish path now has a behavioral gate-passability check, not just the two stage-2/5 checks in `check_scope_root`.

## Vuln 2 — The production `ChildIndexResolver` cannot gate any real descendant scope root; a local capability gap is reported as a forgery verdict — `crates/engine/src/net/adopter.rs:240`

- **Severity: HIGH** · Category: `authorization_logic` / `fail_closed_misclassification` (rule 6) · **Confidence 9 — not fixed, reported**
- **Description:** `gated_root` (`net/rotation.rs:152-159`) builds a `RootAdopter`, whose `ReaderContext` hardcodes `parent_node_seed: None`. The gate treats a *present* `ascent_link` with no reader parent seed as a fail-closed trust violation — `AscentLinkMismatch`, stage `GrantSection` (`gate/adoption.rs:508-516`). But **every interior scope root carries an ascent link**: `reseal_scope_root` authors one whenever `parent_node_seed` is `Some` (`reseal.rs:322`), and both scope-minting paths pass `Some` — `grants/create.rs:353` and `rotation/cascade.rs:525`. Descendants in the eager set are by definition interior scope roots.
- **Impact:** `direct_child_index` returns `ResolveFailure::Rejected` for the first real descendant, `enumerate_eager_set` aborts fail-closed (`rotation/eager_set.rs:265-272`), and a revocation rotation can **never be proven cut**. Separately, this is a rule-6 misclassification in the wrong direction: a purely local missing-key condition emits `Rejected`, the strongest attributable-abuse signal the walk has, which would misattribute abuse to an honest scope.
- **Why no test caught it:** `owner_root_fixture` always sets `ascent_link: None` (`testkit/owner_root.rs:181`), so `the_eager_set_walk_composes_over_the_production_resolver` walks two roots no production path would ever produce. `adopter.rs:240` is the engine's only non-test `ReaderContext`, and this slice is its first caller that can meet an ascent-link-bearing record.
- **Why not fixed here:** not a one-liner. `ChildIndexResolver::direct_child_index(&self, child: &ChildScopeRef)` carries no place to thread the parent node seed the cascade already derives (`cascade.rs:514-515`); this needs a trait-signature change plus an ancestor-seed source, which is a design decision for the slice owner.

## Vuln 3 — A fail-closed gate rejection is laundered into a retryable transport failure — `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:251-253`

- **Severity: MEDIUM** · Category: `fail_closed_misclassification` (rule 6) · Confidence 8
- `gated_root` correctly distinguishes the two verdicts (`rotation.rs:164-167`), and the resolver arm preserves it into `EnumerationError`. The publish arm throws it away: `.map_err(|_| ScopeRootPublishError::NotPublished)`. `NotPublished` is documented "**Retryable**" (`rotation/rotate.rs:71`) and surfaces as `RotateError::Publish` = "nothing was cut, retry later". A forged, tampered, or transplanted scope-root record is therefore indistinguishable from a flaky endpoint, and the host retries against attacker-held bytes indefinitely with no abuse signal. `rotation.rs:245` collapses the same way — a non-canonical `ipnsName` is an explicit fail-closed rejection in the resolver arm (`rotation.rs:93-98`) but becomes `NotPublished` here. **Recommendation:** give `ScopeRootPublishError` a third, non-retryable trust variant mirroring `ResolveFailure::Rejected`.

## Vuln 4 — The outgoing grant-set commitment's signature is never verified encode-side — `crates/engine/src/net/author.rs:162-170`

- **Severity: MEDIUM** · Category: `fail_closed_asymmetry` (rule 8) · Confidence 8
- `check_scope_root` enforces only the *name* half of gate stage 2. The gate's other stage-2 reject, `verify_grant_set(owner_identity, &section.commitment, &commitment_sig)` (`gate/adoption.rs:442`), has no encode-side mirror on this path — `reseal_scope_root` copies `commitment` and `commitment_sig` through verbatim (`reseal.rs:388-390`) without verifying them. `publish_scope_root` holds the owner verifier (`keys.identity`, used at `rotation.rs:157`) and never applies it to the record it signs. Any caller drift between `plan.committed.commitment` and `.commitment_sig` yields another signed, published, permanently unopenable root. Distinct from the committed-pseudonym check already enforced at `reseal.rs:206` and from `enforce_committed_ledger`. Note that Vuln 1's new re-adopt test would now catch this class in the harness, but a release-active check on the publish path is still the right guard.

## Vuln 5 — `record.write_epoch` is never read, and `record.read_epoch` is never checked against the durable floor — `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:240-311`

- **Severity: LOW–MEDIUM** · Category: `fail_closed_asymmetry` · Confidence 7
- `ResealedScopeRoot.write_epoch` is used nowhere in the impl. The signer is derived from `current.write_scope_seed`, recovered by opening the *current* record's owner-write-blob at AAD epoch = `write_epoch_floor(scope_id)` (`net/adopter.rs:314-338`), while the section being published seals its write-body and owner-write-blob at `record.write_epoch` (`reseal.rs:296`, `:371-378`). Nothing compares them, though `self.floors` is in hand at `rotation.rs:187`. On divergence the root publishes write-plane-dead: held keyless forever, `direct_child_scope_index` unreadable, and un-rotatable (floors are monotonic, so a `write_epoch < floor` is permanent). Symmetrically, `record.read_epoch` (`:266`, `:281`) is never compared to `read_epoch_floor`, so a plan built from a stale snapshot publishes an `epoch-below-floor` root while `rotate_scope` reports success. Two cheap release-active equality checks close both.

---

## Checked and clean — no finding

- **Input binding / `ChildScopeRef.scope_id`:** genuinely **imposed**, not network-influenced. It flows `child.scope_id` → `RootAdopter::root_scope_id` (`rotation.rs:158`) → `ReaderContext.scope_id` → the stage-5 floor key and the stage-6 rejection `candidate.envelope.scope != reader.scope_id` (`gate/adoption.rs:572`). Covered by `a_record_claiming_another_scope_is_a_fail_closed_rejection`. Deeper levels come only from a gate-passed, structure-signed, AEAD-sealed write body, with cross-parent label agreement enforced by `bind_child_labels`.
- **Under-enumeration:** no new vector. Every failure path returns `Err`, never `Ok(vec![])` — notably the "held keyless" path returns `Err(Unavailable)` rather than an empty index, which is the one place a silent revocation hole could have hidden.
- **Lost race / unconfirmed publish:** correctly distinguished and never a false success (`rotation.rs:304-310`); `Unconfirmed` is properly refused. Covered by `a_concurrent_writer_at_a_higher_sequence_is_a_retryable_lost_race`.
- **Determinism seams:** the per-seal nonce comes from the injected `Entropy` seam (`rotation.rs:126-133`); no clock or RNG is reached for.

`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a31f1ad63f0ca0571/crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:168-189` — `mint_invite_grant` is a verbatim re-derivation of `create_read_grant` step 3.

Cost: the invite is a special case *by construction of a parallel code path*, even though its runtime behaviour is generic. If the pseudonym-derivation input or the tag input ever changes on the personal path, invites silently derive a tag nobody can self-locate, and the type system says nothing. The tell is in the tests: `invite.rs:227-245` (`fn personal_grant`) is a **third** hand-written copy of the same derivation, because the test cannot call the real personal-grant path to compare against. A test that has to re-implement the thing it's comparing to is not proving byte-shape equality; it's proving the author copied correctly twice.

Deeper fix: `InviteGrant { tag, commitment_entry, ledger_entry }` (invite.rs:137-146) is *already* the right primitive — it is a generic "grant row pair", misnamed for its first caller. Lift it to `ledger.rs` (or a `grants::row` module) as `GrantRow` + `fn mint_grant_row(owner_enc_secret, recipient_identity_pk, recipient_enc_pub, scope_id, name, permission, expires_at)`. `create_read_grant` step 3 becomes a call with `expires_at: None`; `invite.rs` becomes ~15 lines (`EphemeralInvitee` + a thin wrapper). <result>Review complete. Ran the diff, the binding docs (`AGENTS.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `blueprint/engine.md` "Invites"), issue #1015, and verified one finding empirically with a throwaway probe crate against the branch's `crates/core` (scratchpad only — nothing in the worktree was touched).

## REAL findings

### P1 — Encode/decode asymmetry: `expiresAt: 0` can still be encoded, via `unknown` (AGENTS.md rule 8)

**Files:** `crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs:69` (`check_expiry`), `:119-138` (`to_value`), `:243-248` (`encode_write_body`); `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:477-483` (`merge_unknown`)

`expires_at` is the **first and only** conditionally-inserted typed field anywhere in `crates/core/src/seal/*.rs` (grep confirms). `merge_unknown`'s skip-on-collision guard only fires when the typed field is already in the map — so when `expires_at == None`, nothing occupies the `"expiresAt"` key and a caller-built `PreservedFields` carrying it is merged in verbatim. `encode_write_body`'s new `check_expiry` loop only inspects the *typed* field, so it passes.

`body.rs:474-476` explicitly documents the opposite: *"the skip-on-collision guard is for the construction path: a caller-built `unknown` list carrying a schema key can never overwrite the typed value and forge bytes that disagree with it."* That claim is now false for this field.

Verified empirically (probe crate, path-dep on this branch's core):

```
GrantLedgerEntry { expires_at: None, unknown: ["expiresAt" -> Unsigned(0)], .. }
→ encoded 225 bytes
→ ASYMMETRY CONFIRMED: decode rejects with check = invalid-expiry
```

**Failure mode:** a release build encodes, seals, structure-signs and publishes a write-body that every honest decoder rejects `invalid-expiry` — an unopenable scope-root write-body until an owner rotation. Exactly the class rule 8 exists to close.

**Reachability, honestly:** latent, not attacker-reachable today. `PreservedFields::insert` is `pub(crate)`, but the `FromIterator` impl (`body.rs:443`) is public and `codec::Value` is public, so any engine-side caller can build it. The decode path can never populate it (`"expiresAt"` is now in `LEDGER_ENTRY_KNOWN`, `write_body.rs:57`), so hostile bytes cannot round-trip into this.

**Fix (preferred, kills the class):** give `merge_unknown` the known-key list and skip every known key, not just keys present in the map — that restores the documented invariant for any future `Option` field. **Minimal fix:** extend `check_expiry` / the `encode_write_body` loop to also `Err(InvalidExpiry)` when `entry.unknown.get("expiresAt").is_some()`. Either way add a release-active test.

### P2 — `scope_root_ipns_name` is accepted as raw input, against the sibling mint's own fail-closed convention

**Files:** `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:154-172` vs `crates/engine/src/grants/create.rs:60-64` and `:297-304`

`create_read_grant` **derives** the scope root's name (`derive_write_name(write_scope_seed, scope_id)`) and its doc says why in as many words: *"never accepted as input: the blinded tag and the commitment both bind that name, so binding them to anything but the folder's real resolvable name … would mint a grant the recipient can never self-locate."* `mint_invite_grant` takes `scope_root_ipns_name: &[u8]` unvalidated and re-states that identical hazard as a doc-comment warning at `:154-156` instead of enforcing it. Empty-name is also accepted (`blinded_tag(shared, b"")` yields a well-formed tag).

Classification of the inputs: `owner_enc_secret` trusted (owner-held), `invitee` bound (derived in-module), `permission` trusted, `expires_at` validated (`:165`), `scope_root_ipns_name` **unbound**, `scope_id` **unbound**.

**Failure mode:** not a confidentiality break — the tag is public, and a wrong name yields a tag that self-locates in no record (fail-safe: a silently dead invite link). It is an integration hazard the sibling function deliberately designed out.

Also unstated: `scope_id` (`:160`, used at `:173` for the pseudonym) and `scope_root_ipns_name` (`:161`, used at `:172` for the tag) must name the *same* scope root; nothing binds or documents that coupling. A mismatch commits a pseudonym the bearer derives differently.

**Fix:** take the scope root's write-scope seed and derive the name in-function as `create_read_grant` does; at minimum reject an empty name and document the `scope_id`/name coupling on the `scope_id` parameter.

### P2 — Ledger expiry has no production reader; `entry_is_live` is exported but never called on a read path

**File:** `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:76-81`

Grep over `crates/`, `packages/`, `apps/`: every call site is a test. `decode_write_body` has no caller in `crates/engine/src/` at all — the gate (`crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:491-492`) only verifies the write-body's structure signature, never opens it. So a minted deadline is currently honoured by nobody, and #1015's stated gate criterion *"an expired ledger entry is inert on the read path even before the discovered-expiry trigger prunes it"* is not met by this PR.

This is consistent with #1015's declared two-PR split (this is PR (a)), and the prune trigger is tracked separately as #1020 — but the read-path predicate itself has no tracked wiring issue that I could find. **Fix:** confirm #1016 (facade command arms) or PR (b) covers calling `entry_is_live` on the resolve/accept path, and add a dependency edge; a shipped-but-unread expiry field is a false sense of security if a host UI starts minting expiring links first.

### nit — `from_secret` doesn't state who owns zeroization of the caller's buffer

`crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:100` takes `&[u8; SECRET_LEN]` — a plain array the callee copies. The terminal-owner rule holds (see below), but the signature invites a link-fragment parser to leave the raw secret unzeroized. One line on the parameter would close it. Compare `mint` at `:88`, which does it correctly with `Zeroizing`.

**Location:** `crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs:119-138` and `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:472-483`.

```rust
// body.rs:472-477 — "typed fields taking precedence … a caller-built `unknown`
// list carrying a schema key can never overwrite the typed value and forge bytes
// that disagree with it."
pub(super) fn merge_unknown(map: &mut Map, unknown: &PreservedFields) {
    for (k, v) in unknown.entries() {
        if !map.contains_key(k) { map.insert(k.clone(), v.clone()); }
    }
}
```

Every other key in `LEDGER_ENTRY_KNOWN` is unconditionally inserted, so `contains_key` always fires. `expiresAt` is inserted only `if let Some(..)` (`write_body.rs:121`). With `expires_at: None` there is **no collision**, and the unknown-field copy is merged verbatim. `PreservedFields: FromIterator<(String, Value)>` is public API (`body.rs:443`), so this is constructible by any engine caller:

```rust
let e = GrantLedgerEntry {
    expires_at: None,
    unknown: PreservedFields::from_iter([("expiresAt".to_string(), Value::Unsigned(0))]),
    ..GrantLedgerEntry::new(id_pk, enc_pk, Permission::Read, tag)
};
let bytes = encode_write_body(&body).unwrap();          // Ok — check_expiry saw None
decode_write_body(&bytes).unwrap_err().check();          // "invalid-expiry"
```

That is AGENTS.md rule 8 verbatim: a release build seals, signs, and publishes a write-body its own decoder always rejects — an unopenable scope root, i.e. a self-inflicted denial of the write plane. The non-zero variant is worse in kind: `("expiresAt", Unsigned(<future>))` encodes a deadline the typed struct says does not exist, so the mint signs a ledger asserting an expiry it never authorized, and every in-process check (`entry_is_live`, the mint's `InvalidExpiry` guard) reasons over the `None` that is not what was sealed.

The in-flight `NonZeroU64` refactor does **not** fix this — it removes the typed zero, not the `unknown`-channel zero.

```rust
// body.rs
pub(super) fn assert_unknown_disjoint(u: &PreservedFields, known: &[&str]) -> Result<(), CodecError> {
    match u.entries().iter().find(|(k, _)| known.contains(&k.as_str())) {
        Some(_) => Err(Malformed::UnexpectedType.into()), // or a dedicated verdict
        None => Ok(()),
    }
}
// encode_write_body: per ledger entry
assert_unknown_disjoint(&entry.unknown, LEDGER_ENTRY_KNOWN)?;
```

## CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT

**1. KDF edge discipline — sound, and the right call.** Reusing `enc-subkey` with an ephemeral ikm is **not** a cross-protocol hazard, for three reasons. (a) The edge's frozen layout is `derive_key(ctx, loginSecret[var])`; a 32-byte ephemeral secret satisfies `[var]`, so no layout is violated and no edge is invented. (b) Domain separation in this catalog lives in the BLAKE3 context string, not in the ikm's provenance — `derive_key` is a PRF keyed by context, so independent ikms give independent outputs regardless of what the ikm "is." A collision with a real user's `enc-subkey` requires an invite secret equal to a login secret: 2^-256. (c) The composite shape — one 32-byte value serving verbatim as a secp256k1 scalar *and* as BLAKE3 ikm — is not new: it is the frozen login-secret shape imposed by the Web3Auth TSS export (`session.rs:53-59`), and the freeze forbids minting an `invite-identity` edge to separate them. Adopting the scalar directly is therefore the only catalog-compliant option, and it is precisely what makes the ephemeral identity *structurally* a login identity — which is what buys the blob indistinguishability the design depends on. Knowledge of `P = sG` (secp256k1) and `Q = X25519(derive_key(ctx, s))` yields no relation between them; signatures are RFC 6979 deterministic and leak nothing about `s`. **Verdict: sound. No new edge, no key-reuse hazard, no downgrade.** The residual is one-directional and inherent: leaking the fragment leaks both halves — which is the definition of a bearer credential.

**2. Ephemeral key hygiene.** `mint` draws from the injected `Entropy` seam (`invite.rs:89-95`), never a direct RNG, and the test at `invite.rs:308-317` proves the secret is byte-for-byte the seam's output. Entropy failure is fail-closed with a typed error and is tested with a `DryEntropy` stub. The no-re-sample choice is **correct and unbiased**: failing on an invalid scalar and rejection-sampling produce the identical conditional distribution over accepted keys, so nothing is weakened; failing closed additionally keeps the entropy budget fixed. `EcdsaSigner::from_scalar` correctly rejects zero and ≥ n (`ecdsa.rs:42-44`), and the zero-scalar case is tested.

**3. Blob indistinguishability, envelope surface.** Verified against `reseal.rs:233-271` and `grant.rs`: one blob per ledger row, blobs sorted by tag (explicitly so wire order leaks no ledger order), the same `GrantBlobPayload` shape for equal permissions, the same owner pseudonym signature. `GrantSetEntry` for an invite is byte-identical to a personal grantee's. The `expiresAt` field is confined to the sealed write-body, and the test at `invite.rs:374-379` proves the deadline does not appear in the plaintext envelope. The only observable is the write-body length (F6).

AAD context is `{v, id, scope, epoch, struct_tag}` per structure, and the test at `invite.rs:427-452` proves the blob's structure signature and AAD-bound unseal both verify for the fragment holder. ### [P1] `expiresAt` is an unauthenticated field that any write-grantee controls

**Location:** `crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs:46-52`; `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:76-81`; `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:180-188`; gap surface at `crates/core/src/seal/grant.rs:670-681` (`GrantSetEntry` = `{tag, permission, pseudonymPk}`) and `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:120-124`.

**Failure mode.** The grant ledger lives in the sealed write-body, which every write-grantee re-authors on every re-seal. `enforce_committed_ledger` compares only `(tag → permission)`; the owner's ECDSA signature covers only `GrantSetEntry`. So `expiresAt` is the one ledger field with **no owner authentication and no cross-check**. Two concrete abuses:

1. **Self-extension.** A `Permission::Write` invite holder receives `writeScopeSeed` in its own grant blob (`reseal.rs:239-242`), therefore holds `writeKey` and can re-seal the write-body under a committed pseudonym. It drops its own row's `expiresAt`. `enforce_committed_ledger` passes; the structure signature verifies; the adoption gate adopts. The deadline the owner set on a **bearer** credential is erased by the bearer. Blueprint anticipates this for write links ("revoking or expiring one is only real via write rotation") but the diff's own doc comment does not.
2. **Induced revocation (the novel direction).** A write-grantee *adds* `expiresAt: <past>` to a **victim's** row. Blueprint says expiry is "lazily pruned via the discovered-expiry trigger". If the owner's client auto-prunes on discovered expiry, a write-grantee has just acquired a lever on the owner's re-signed commitment — converting "cutting a grantee off is owner-only" into "any write-grantee can induce a revocation of any other grantee." Because invite rows are byte-indistinguishable from personal rows by design, **no client can tell that a row was never supposed to carry a deadline**, so the tamper is undetectable in principle, not just in practice.

**Impact:** privilege extension on a bearer credential; escalation of write-grantee authority into owner-only revocation authority.

**Fix (structural):** add the deadline to the owner-signed commitment and to the authority comparison. This is compatible with the "deliberately epoch-free" commitment property — expiry is minted once by the owner and is invariant across rotations, so it introduces no owner signature on a grantee-triggered rotation.

```rust
    owner_enc_secret: &X25519Secret,
    invitee: &EphemeralInvitee,
    scope_id: &[u8; 16],
    write_scope_seed: &[u8; SECRET_LEN],   // derive, never accept
```

**Location:** `crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs:119-138` and `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:472-483`.

`merge_unknown` documents the exact invariant this breaks:

```rust
// body.rs:472-477 — "typed fields taking precedence … a caller-built `unknown`
// list carrying a schema key can never overwrite the typed value and forge bytes
// that disagree with it."
pub(super) fn merge_unknown(map: &mut Map, unknown: &PreservedFields) {
    for (k, v) in unknown.entries() {
        if !map.contains_key(k) { map.insert(k.clone(), v.clone()); }
    }
}
```

Every other key in `LEDGER_ENTRY_KNOWN` is unconditionally inserted, so `contains_key` always fires. `expiresAt` is inserted only `if let Some(..)` (`write_body.rs:121`). With `expires_at: None` there is **no collision**, and the unknown-field copy is merged verbatim. `PreservedFields: FromIterator<(String, Value)>` is public API (`body.rs:443`), so this is constructible by any engine caller:

```rust
let e = GrantLedgerEntry {
    expires_at: None,
    unknown: PreservedFields::from_iter([("expiresAt".to_string(), Value::Unsigned(0))]),
    ..GrantLedgerEntry::new(id_pk, enc_pk, Permission::Read, tag)
};
let bytes = encode_write_body(&body).unwrap();          // Ok — check_expiry saw None
decode_write_body(&bytes).unwrap_err().check();          // "invalid-expiry"
```

That is AGENTS.md rule 8 verbatim: a release build seals, signs, and publishes a write-body its own decoder always rejects — an unopenable scope root, i.e. a self-inflicted denial of the write plane. The non-zero variant is worse in kind: `("expiresAt", Unsigned(<future>))` encodes a deadline the typed struct says does not exist, so the mint signs a ledger asserting an expiry it never authorized, and every in-process check (`entry_is_live`, the mint's `InvalidExpiry` guard) reasons over the `None` that is not what was sealed.

The in-flight `NonZeroU64` refactor does **not** fix this — it removes the typed zero, not the `unknown`-channel zero.

**Fix:** a release-active disjointness guard, applied wherever an optional known key exists:

```rust
// body.rs
pub(super) fn assert_unknown_disjoint(u: &PreservedFields, known: &[&str]) -> Result<(), CodecError> {
    match u.entries().iter().find(|(k, _)| known.contains(&k.as_str())) {
        Some(_) => Err(Malformed::UnexpectedType.into()), // or a dedicated verdict
        None => Ok(()),
    }
}
// encode_write_body: per ledger entry
assert_unknown_disjoint(&entry.unknown, LEDGER_ENTRY_KNOWN)?;
```

**Related, pre-existing, out of this diff but the same class and worth filing:** `crates/core/src/seal/grant.rs:181` makes `writeScopeSeed` conditional in `encode_grant_blob_payload` and then calls `merge_unknown`. A caller-built `unknown` carrying `writeScopeSeed` on a `Permission::Read` payload injects a write seed into a sealed read grant. That argues for the shared helper rather than a local patch.

**Location:** `crates/core/src/error.rs:305-307`, `crates/core/src/seal/write_body.rs:65-68`, `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:56-58`, and the KAT reject-vector comment in `crates/core/examples/kat_gen.rs`.

> "absence is the only encoding of 'no deadline', so a zero instant is a second spelling of it that is also permanently expired"

Under `entry_is_live` (`ledger.rs:76-81`), `None` ⇒ **always live** and `Some(0)` ⇒ `now < 0` ⇒ **always dead**. These are opposites, not two spellings of one thing. The reject is defensible on a different ground (0 is the natural uninitialized value, so accepting it makes a bug indistinguishable from intent), but the rationale as written is normative — it is replicated into a **frozen KAT reject vector** and the `Malformed::InvalidExpiry` doc. An auditor reading it concludes `0 ≡ None`; anyone "simplifying" the codec on that reading maps `0 → None` and turns an always-dead row into a never-expiring one — a fail-open edit licensed by the comment. Note also that the rule rejects exactly one of 2^64−1 already-expired encodings: `Some(1)` is accepted and permanently dead. State the real reason and drop the false equivalence.

### [P2] The sealed write-body's *length* discriminates an expiring row

**Location:** claim at `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:8-12`; test at `invite.rs:343-380`.

Envelope-surface indistinguishability holds and is well tested: blobs are sorted by tag (`reseal.rs:271`), the commitment entry is byte-identical, blob/`enc`/signature lengths match, and the deadline is verified absent from the plaintext envelope. But the sealed write-body's ciphertext length is a public observable, and every non-expiring ledger row is fixed-width (32+33+32 bytes plus a `read`/`write` discriminant). An `expiresAt` row adds ~19 bytes. An observer watching successive re-seals of one scope root sees a per-row length step that differs for expiring rows — so the number of expiry-bearing (i.e. almost certainly invite) rows leaks up to the noise of `writeHistoryLink` and `directChildScopeIndex`. Second-order, and it requires longitudinal observation, but the module header states the indistinguishability claim without scoping it.

**Fix:** scope the claim to the grant-blob/commitment surface in the module doc, and add a length-bucketed pad to the write-body plaintext before sealing if the leak matters. Add a test asserting the current delta so the observable is pinned rather than folklore.

### [P2] `EphemeralInvitee` holds the raw invite scalar twice and is `Clone`

**Location:** `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:38-43`, `100-107`.

`secret: SecretBytes` is the raw secp256k1 scalar; `identity: EcdsaSigner` wraps `SigningKey`, which is *the same scalar again*. `#[derive(Clone)]` doubles both per clone. Each copy is an independent zeroizing owner, so nothing leaks on drop, but for a bearer capability the live-copy count is the exposure surface (core dumps, WASM linear memory, JS heap snapshots).

**Fix:** drop the `secret` field and expose the fragment bytes from the signer (`SigningKey::to_bytes()`), leaving one copy; and drop `Clone` unless a caller needs it — nothing in the diff clones an `EphemeralInvitee`.

Related note, no code change requested: `secret()` is fully `pub` (unlike `SessionIdentity`, whose secret-bearing accessors are `pub(crate)`). That is necessary — the fragment must reach the user — but it means the invite secret crosses the WASM boundary into an unzeroizable JS `Uint8Array`. Worth a host-facing note that the fragment must never be logged, never sent to the API, and never placed anywhere but the URL fragment (which is correctly chosen: fragments are not transmitted in the request line or `Referer`).

### [P2] An invite secret is a fully functional account credential

**Location:** `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:100-107`.

`EphemeralInvitee` is byte-for-byte the same construction as `SessionIdentity::derive` (`session.rs:74-83`) — scalar adopted directly as the secp256k1 identity, `enc-subkey` for the sealing half. That is what buys the indistinguishability, and it is the right call (see the verdict below). The consequence is unstated anywhere: **the bearer of an invite link can complete the API's challenge-signature login with the ephemeral identity and enroll a phantom account.** Not a cryptographic break — anyone can generate a keypair — but any API-side logic that reads "an identity that authenticated" as "a person" now includes throwaway invite identities, and the invite's `recipientIdentityPk` sits in a ledger with no contact-code binding signature behind it. Document it at the type, and confirm the registry/mailbox side does not treat a ledger `recipientIdentityPk` as a bound identity.

### [P2] One `EphemeralInvitee` is reusable across scopes, and the API does not discourage it

**Location:** `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs:157-190`.

The pairwise material is correctly re-derived per call, so nothing collides: `tag` binds `scope_root_ipns_name`, `pseudonym_sign` binds `scope_id`. But the ledger row's `recipientIdentityPk`/`recipientEncPk` are the *same bytes* in both scopes, so anyone who can read both write-bodies (the owner, and any write-grantee of both) links the two grants to one link — defeating the writer-pseudonym property that "observers see nothing linkable across scopes" for exactly this recipient class. And one leaked fragment then unseals both scopes.

**Fix:** take the invitee by value (`invitee: EphemeralInvitee`) so reuse is at least visible at the call site, or mint the invitee inside `mint_invite_grant` from the entropy seam and return the secret alongside the grant.

### [nit] Two imprecise claims worth one line each

- `invite.rs:85-88`: "never by re-sampling until one lands, which would make the mint non-deterministic in its injected entropy." Re-sampling from an injected seam is still deterministic; the honest reason is that it makes the entropy *budget* variable, desynchronizing every downstream draw. Say that.
- The ~2^-128 rejection probability is never quantified anywhere. One line (`SigningKey::from_slice` rejects zero and ≥ n; P ≈ 2^-128 for secp256k1) turns "vanishing chance" into an auditable claim.

## CHECKED AND FOUND CORRECT

**1. KDF edge discipline — sound, and the right call.** Reusing `enc-subkey` with an ephemeral ikm is **not** a cross-protocol hazard, for three reasons. (a) The edge's frozen layout is `derive_key(ctx, loginSecret[var])`; a 32-byte ephemeral secret satisfies `[var]`, so no layout is violated and no edge is invented. (b) Domain separation in this catalog lives in the BLAKE3 context string, not in the ikm's provenance — `derive_key` is a PRF keyed by context, so independent ikms give independent outputs regardless of what the ikm "is." A collision with a real user's `enc-subkey` requires an invite secret equal to a login secret: 2^-256. (c) The composite shape — one 32-byte value serving verbatim as a secp256k1 scalar *and* as BLAKE3 ikm — is not new: it is the frozen login-secret shape imposed by the Web3Auth TSS export (`session.rs:53-59`), and the freeze forbids minting an `invite-identity` edge to separate them. Adopting the scalar directly is therefore the only catalog-compliant option, and it is precisely what makes the ephemeral identity *structurally* a login identity — which is what buys the blob indistinguishability the design depends on. Knowledge of `P = sG` (secp256k1) and `Q = X25519(derive_key(ctx, s))` yields no relation between them; signatures are RFC 6979 deterministic and leak nothing about `s`. **Verdict: sound. No new edge, no key-reuse hazard, no downgrade.** The residual is one-directional and inherent: leaking the fragment leaks both halves — which is the definition of a bearer credential.

**2. Ephemeral key hygiene.** `mint` draws from the injected `Entropy` seam (`invite.rs:89-95`), never a direct RNG, and the test at `invite.rs:308-317` proves the secret is byte-for-byte the seam's output. Entropy failure is fail-closed with a typed error and is tested with a `DryEntropy` stub. The no-re-sample choice is **correct and unbiased**: failing on an invalid scalar and rejection-sampling produce the identical conditional distribution over accepted keys, so nothing is weakened; failing closed additionally keeps the entropy budget fixed. `EcdsaSigner::from_scalar` correctly rejects zero and ≥ n (`ecdsa.rs:42-44`), and the zero-scalar case is tested.

**3. Blob indistinguishability, envelope surface.** Verified against `reseal.rs:233-271` and `grant.rs`: one blob per ledger row, blobs sorted by tag (explicitly so wire order leaks no ledger order), the same `GrantBlobPayload` shape for equal permissions, the same owner pseudonym signature. `GrantSetEntry` for an invite is byte-identical to a personal grantee's. The `expiresAt` field is confined to the sealed write-body, and the test at `invite.rs:374-379` proves the deadline does not appear in the plaintext envelope. The only observable is the write-body length (F6).

**4. AAD / binding.** `mint_invite_grant` derives `tag = blinded_tag(ECDH(ownerEnc, inviteeEnc), scopeRootIpnsName)` and `pseudonym = pseudonym_sign(shared, scopeId)` — identical to `create_read_grant:311-318`. Non-contributory ECDH is rejected via `X25519Secret::diffie_hellman`'s `was_contributory` check (`x25519.rs:44-50`), mapped to `UnusableInviteeKey`. AAD context is `{v, id, scope, epoch, struct_tag}` per structure, and the test at `invite.rs:427-452` proves the blob's structure signature and AAD-bound unseal both verify for the fragment holder. Owner-only authority is enforced ahead of any seal by `SignerNotCommitted` (`reseal.rs:207-211`), covered for the invite path by `an_invite_committed_under_a_non_owner_pseudonym_is_refused`.

**5. `entry_is_live` boundary.** `now < expires_at` — dies *at* the deadline, not a tick later; `None` ⇒ live. Boundary is tested at 999/1000/1001. Correct as a predicate. Its problem is the authenticity of its input (F1), not its logic.

**6. Zeroization.** Terminal-owner rule respected. `mint` owns a `Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>` that wipes on scope exit (`invite.rs:90-94`); `from_secret` takes `&[u8; 32]`, copies, and correctly does **not** zero the caller's buffer (`invite.rs:100-107`). `SecretBytes` and `X25519Secret` zeroize on drop with redacted `Debug`. `reseal_scope_root` zeroizes only its own transients (`reseal.rs:251`, `255`, `379`) and documents that borrowed seeds stay the caller's.

**7. Secret leakage.** `EphemeralInvitee`'s derived `Debug` is pinned by a **whole-string** golden (`invite.rs:565-573`) — the strongest form, since any field added later of any type breaks it and forces a redaction decision. `InviteError::check()` returns fixed classification names; `Display` prints only `check()`; the wrapped `EntropyError` carries a caller-supplied diagnostic string only. `AuthorityViolation`'s descriptions carry counts, never tags. No path logs or returns key material.

**8. Constant time.** The distinction is drawn correctly throughout. Public values use variable-time compares with the reason stated: blinded tags in `self_locate` (`ledger.rs:59-67`), the pseudonym public key in `reseal.rs:205-208`, `GrantSetEntry`/`GrantLedgerEntry` derived `PartialEq`. Secrets use `ct_eq`/`SecretBytes::eq`: `invite.rs:300`, `314`, `453`, and every seed assertion in `reseal.rs`. `EphemeralInvitee` deliberately does **not** derive `PartialEq`, so no secret-comparison footgun exists. `entry_is_live`'s `u64` compare is over data only a legitimate write-plane holder can read.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:

# CipherBox - AI Agent Instructions

## Project Context

CipherBox is a privacy-first, zero-knowledge E2EE personal cloud storage system on IPFS/IPNS. The repo is mid-rewrite: **v2 is being built on `main`** against the blueprint corpus below; v1 is frozen on branch `v1` (tag `v1-freeze`) and receives no changes.

## Documentation Structure

The normative source of truth for the v2 build:

| Document                  | Purpose                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CONTEXT.md`              | The v2 ubiquitous language — use these terms, exactly         |
| `blueprint/core.md`       | `crates/core` — wire formats, crypto, KDF catalog, KAT regime |
| `blueprint/engine.md`     | `crates/engine` — the one stateful brain, seam traits, gates  |
| `blueprint/api.md`        | API residual surface, registry, mailbox, republisher          |
| `blueprint/web-client.md` | WASM hosting, tab leadership, `packages/client`, `apps/web`   |
| `blueprint/desktop.md`    | FS projection, host adapters, Tauri shell                     |
| `blueprint/testing.md`    | Suite map, CI gates, coverage policy                          |
| `blueprint/deploy.md`     | Freeze mechanics, release management, staging pipeline        |

The as-built v1 spec corpus, ADRs, and all design-decision history live in [FSM1/cipher-box-next](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next) (wayfinder map issue 1 indexes every decision). The `docs/` folder is v1 legacy — being rewritten during the build; trust `blueprint/` when they conflict.

## Terminology Standards

Use the v2 ubiquitous language defined in `CONTEXT.md` — every domain term (scope, epoch, ascent link, grant blob, adoption gate, floor law, eager set, …) has exactly one name there. General conventions: `publicKey`/`privateKey`/`ipnsName`/`ipnsRecord` spelled out in full camelCase for API fields, snake_case for database columns.

## Critical Security Rules

1. **Never** store `privateKey` or any seed in localStorage/sessionStorage
2. **Never** log sensitive keys or seeds
3. **Never** send unencrypted keys to the server — the server is zero-knowledge and NEVER sees plaintext or unencrypted keys
4. **All crypto lives in `crates/core`** — TypeScript has no codec or crypto of its own; never implement crypto in TS
5. Primitives are fixed by `blueprint/core.md`: XChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing, BLAKE3 tree KDF, X25519 + HPKE key wrapping, REDACTED signing — no key derives outside the frozen KDF edge catalog
6. Every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness
7. Clear sensitive material from memory after use (zeroize at the terminal owner only — a callee must not zero caller-owned buffers)
8. **Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry** — when a decode/verify path hard-rejects an invariant violation (a trust/malformed check), the matching encode/produce path MUST enforce the same invariant with a **release-active** check that returns `Err` — never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`, which are stripped in release. Otherwise a release build can sign and publish bytes its own decoder always rejects (an unopenable ledger/commitment/body). Keep these encode-side checks consistent with the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention, and cover them with a test that fires in a release build.

## API Contract and Clients

There are **no generated API clients** and no codegen loop. The engine contains the single hand-written Rust API client; the NestJS API's OpenAPI document is a committed docs artifact, not a build input. The contract is enforced by the live contract-test suite (the sdk-e2e descendant) running the real client against a real API instance on every PR — see `blueprint/testing.md`.

## Code Generation Guidelines

1. All engine, codec, and crypto logic is Rust (`crates/core`, `crates/engine`); TypeScript exists only in `packages/client` (WASM wrapper, browser seams) and `apps/web` (React UI)
2. Use `Uint8Array`/`Vec<u8>` for binary data, not strings
3. Determinism is injected: entropy, time, and policy enter as parameters/seam traits — never call clocks or RNGs directly in core/engine logic
4. Every suite must block a merge in a named CI gate the day it lands (`blueprint/testing.md` law 1); assert behavior, never source text

## Code Style

### Comments

Comments explain _why_, not _what_, and stay short. **If you need a paragraph-long comment to justify why a workaround is OK, the code is wrong — fix the code.** A long apologia for a hack is a smell: rework the code so it no longer needs defending, rather than documenting the shortcut. Reserve multi-line comments for genuinely non-obvious domain rationale — a spec citation, a cryptographic invariant, a wire-format or fail-closed constraint — not for excusing a shortcut.

Two recurring shapes of this smell go beyond excusing a hack — avoid both:

- **Absence-justifying comments** — prose explaining why a path that is _not_ in the code does not happen (e.g. "`replay()` does not run here, so `decode_queue` is the only source at this stage"). It bloats the diff and rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired — a stale in-code claim that actively misleads. Describe what the present code does; a bare cross-reference suffices if a reader must know a related path lives elsewhere.
- **Unchanged-code apologia** — a doc block defending code this change does not modify (e.g. why a parameter stays a raw borrow, on a function the diff leaves untouched). It is scope creep into untouched code and reads as pre-emptive defensiveness. Leave that rationale where it already lives.

State genuine non-obvious domain rationale **once**, at its home (the type or definition), not restated on every caller. These cost real review cycles — `/simplify`, CodeRabbit, and Greptile all flag them.

Length discipline for the permitted domain-rationale exception: state each invariant **once** and prefer a one-line cross-reference to the blueprint / `CONTEXT.md` over re-deriving it in prose. Do not narrate the happy path — the code is the narrative, and a comment restating what the next lines plainly do rots out of sync and misleads. A module header past ~25 lines is almost always restating the spec: keep only the rationale that is non-obvious _from the code itself_ and cite the blueprint for the rest.

## Architecture Pillars

- **Auth:** Web3Auth key derivation; challenge-signature login; short-lived JWT + rotating refresh
- **Storage:** IPFS content, IPNS metadata — the network is canonical; clients verify records cryptographically; CipherBox infra (Kubo, someguy) is accelerator-only and the API never serves records
- **Keys:** seeded per-scope derivation with key-regression epochs; rotation = O(1) root cut + lazy wave (`CONTEXT.md`)
- **One Rust core:** desktop links it natively, web loads it as WASM in a worker; one implementation, one KAT set
- **Sync:** pull-only focus-window polling, cache-first, offline op queue; no push in v2.0 (seam ready)
- **Desktop:** Tauri + FUSE mount (FUSE-T SMB on macOS, libfuse3 on Linux, WinFsp on Windows)
- **No TEE:** the republisher is a keyless re-PUT module inside the API; client-signed 90-day EOLs

## Out of Scope

- Billing/payments, mobile apps, real-time collaborative editing, team accounts
- Vault import (cut in v2), client-side search (deferred, designed-for)
- Executing anything against the frozen `v1` branch

## Verification with MCP Tools

### Puppeteer MCP Verification (REQUIRED)

**ALWAYS attempt to verify application changes using Puppeteer MCP** when it is available. This ensures implemented features work correctly at runtime.

**When to use Puppeteer MCP:**

- After implementing UI components
- After modifying styles or layouts
- After adding new pages or routes
- After any user-facing changes

**Verification workflow:** the dev server runs at `http://localhost:5173`. Navigate, screenshot, assert the elements and computed styles the change touches, then exercise the interaction. Element waits go through `puppeteer_evaluate` polling — there is no dedicated wait tool.

**If Puppeteer MCP is not available:**

- Document what needs human verification
- Provide manual test steps
- Flag items in VERIFICATION.md

### Pencil Design Files

Pencil design files exist at `designs/*.pen` (with `designs/DESIGN.md`) but are not actively maintained right now. `.pen` files are encrypted: read them only through the Pencil MCP tools — never `Read` or `grep` them directly.

## Git Workflow

### Branch Protection Rules

- **NEVER push directly to `main` branch** - all changes must go through feature branches and PRs
- Create feature branches with descriptive names (e.g., `feat/add-auth`, `fix/ipns-publish`)
- All commits should be made on feature branches first
- Merge to main only via pull requests

### Branch Naming

- `feat/` - New features
- `fix/` - Bug fixes
- `docs/` - Documentation updates
- `refactor/` - Code refactoring
- `chore/` - Maintenance tasks

### Commit Messages

Commits must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format:

```text
type(optional-scope): description

[optional body]
```

Valid types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Any scope string is allowed (e.g., `feat(api): add health endpoint`). A custom commitlint rule additionally rejects parenthesized text in the subject line (it breaks Release Please parsing).

Enforcement: commitlint is configured via `commitlint.config.js`, and PR titles are validated in CI by `.github/workflows/pr-title.yml`. Note that the husky `commit-msg` hook was replaced by an Entire CLI wrapper and currently does not run commitlint locally — follow the format regardless, since CI will reject non-conforming PR titles.

### Mandatory PR Review Flow

Every code PR runs these review gates after it is opened as a **draft**, before it is driven toward merge — mandatory, not optional:

1. `/simplify` — tighten the diff: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, and duplication.
2. `/security-review` — trust boundaries, fail-closed behavior, auth/expiry gates, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, and determinism seams.
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — **required whenever the diff touches crypto**: `crates/core` primitives, key/seal material, or trust-boundary and fail-closed reads.

Run each on the PR's own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and fold real findings back into the code and tests before requesting a CodeRabbit/Greptile review. If a slash-command skill is unavailable in your environment, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead — never skip a gate. Self-review is the floor, not the ceiling: layer an independent reviewer pass on crypto- and trust-critical PRs. A pure documentation change with no code surface is exempt.

### Releases & Versioning

See the `releases` skill (`.claude/skills/releases/SKILL.md`) for the v2 release scheme, version surfaces, staging tag pipeline, and the v1 freeze. Normative source: `blueprint/deploy.md`.

- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)

- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:

Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:

| Step | PR | State against the tree at that point |

| 1 | **#1027** rotation | clean vs current `main` — verified |
| 2 | **#1024** invites | clean vs `main`+#1027 — verified |
